title: The Cowardly Lion, part 1
attribution: From The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum (1900), via Project Gutenberg, in reading order.
body: All this time Dorothy and her companions had been walking through the thick woods. The road was still paved with yellow brick, but these were much covered by dried branches and dead leaves from the trees, and the walking was not at all good.

There were few birds in this part of the forest, for birds love the open country where there is plenty of sunshine. But now and then there came a deep growl from some wild animal hidden among the trees. These sounds made the little girl’s heart beat fast, for she did not know what made them; but Toto knew, and he walked close to Dorothy’s side, and did not even bark in return.
“How long will it be,” the child asked of the Tin Woodman, “before we are out of the forest?”

“I cannot tell,” was the answer, “for I have never been to the Emerald City. But my father went there once, when I was a boy, and he said it was a long journey through a dangerous country, although nearer to the city where Oz dwells the country is beautiful. But I am not afraid so long as I have my oil-can, and nothing can hurt the Scarecrow, while you bear upon your forehead the mark of the Good Witch’s kiss, and that will protect you from harm.”
“But Toto!” said the girl anxiously. “What will protect him?”
“We must protect him ourselves if he is in danger,” replied the Tin Woodman.

Just as he spoke there came from the forest a terrible roar, and the next moment a great Lion bounded into the road. With one blow of his paw he sent the Scarecrow spinning over and over to the edge of the road, and then he struck at the Tin Woodman with his sharp claws. But, to the Lion’s surprise, he could make no impression on the tin, although the Woodman fell over in the road and lay still.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what covered the yellow bricks in this part of the forest?
options: Dried branches and dead leaves
Thick moss and creeping vines
Drifted sand from the desert
Snow that had not yet melted

questions.prompt: Per the passage, why were there few birds in this part of the forest?
options: Birds love the open country where there is sunshine
The wild beasts had driven them all away
The trees bore no fruit for them to eat
The Tin Woodman's axe had frightened them off

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who had been to the Emerald City before?
options: The Tin Woodman's father
The Tin Woodman himself
The Scarecrow's farmer
Nobody in the party

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the Lion do to the Scarecrow?
options: Sent him spinning to the edge of the road
Tore the straw out of his chest
Carried him off among the trees
Knocked his painted hat into the road

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happened when the Lion struck the Tin Woodman?
options: He could make no impression on the tin
He tore a long gash in the tin body
He knocked the axe out of his hands
He bent the tin legs out of shape

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, how does Toto behave when the growls are heard?
options: He keeps close to Dorothy and does not bark back
He runs ahead into the trees to investigate
He barks louder than the beasts themselves
He hides inside Dorothy's basket

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why is the Tin Woodman unafraid of the journey?
options: He has his oil-can, and his companions are protected too
He has been along this road many times already
He believes the Wizard is watching over them
He is certain no beast can be found in the forest

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what is said to protect Dorothy from harm?
options: The mark of the Good Witch's kiss on her forehead
The silver shoes she took from the dead witch
The Tin Woodman's axe and the Scarecrow's strength
The basket she carries from the Munchkin house

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that Dorothy asked anxiously about Toto?
options: She asked out of worry for him
She asked without much interest
She asked to change the subject
She asked in order to boast

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the passage?
options: A talk about who is safe on the road is cut short by an attack
A quiet day's walk through a forest where nothing happens
A decision to leave the forest road and go around it
A warning from the Tin Woodman that they should turn back

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what made Dorothy's heart beat fast?
options: Deep growls from wild animals hidden among the trees
The darkness under the thickly grown branches
The sight of the Lion crossing the road ahead
The Tin Woodman's account of the journey

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the Tin Woodman say about the country nearer the city?
options: That it is beautiful
That it is a desert
That it is thickly forested
That nobody has ever seen it

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Tin Woodman say must be done for Toto?
options: They must protect him themselves
He must be carried in the basket
He must be sent back to the Munchkins
He must be given a mark of his own

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Toto's silence suggest he understands?
options: What the growling animals are, unlike Dorothy
That the Scarecrow is about to be attacked
That the road has been lost among the leaves
That the Tin Woodman cannot be hurt

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Tin Woodman say nothing can hurt the Scarecrow?
options: Being stuffed with straw, he cannot be injured
He is too tall for a beast to reach
He carries the axe when danger comes
The witch's kiss protects him as well

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Lion bounded into the road?
options: He sprang into it in great leaps
He crept into it without a sound
He strolled into it at his leisure
He was driven into it by others

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarises the passage?
options: Reassurance about the dangers ahead, then a sudden attack
A dispute about whether the party should keep to the road
A description of how the forest differs from Munchkin country
An account of the Tin Woodman's father and his travels
